📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the news release, Most Legal Professionals Say AI Has Not Yet Changed Hiring, According to a Relativity Study, issued 12-Nov-2026 by Relativity over PR Newswire, we are advised by the tech giant that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:.

CHICAGO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Relativity, a legal data intelligence company, today announced findings from AI in Legal: 2026 Research Data, with research and analysis by International Data Corporation (IDC), a upcoming study examining how legal professionals are adopting and governing AI. The study combines primary research from IDC, a survey of state court judges conducted by Relativity and the National Association of Women Judges (NAWJ), and findings from the upcoming eighth annual edition of The General Counsel Report, produced by Relativity and FTI Consulting. Together, these perspectives offer a broad view of AI use across the legal landscape, along with the growing importance of trust, governance and accountability.

It has been revealed that the study draws on research conducted from April to October 2026, incorporating feedback from 700 legal professionals across 20 nations, including an IDC study of 401 respondents. Participants included lawyers, paralegals, legal technologists and legal IT professionals. The countries represented are Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China (Hong Kong), Colombia, France, Germany, India, Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Recent findings suggest that "In this 2026 follow-up to our 2024 study, the data show that AI use in the legal profession is now a fait accompli. The question is no longer 'Are legal teams using AI?' but 'How and why are lawyers and their colleagues using it?'" said David Horrigan, Discovery Counsel and Legal Education Director at Relativity. "Some of the data, such as more than 91.0% of chief legal officers and more than 80.0% of all legal professionals using AI, was not surprising at all. What did surprise us was that, for most respondents, AI has had no effect on hiring at this point, and more reported adding staff than cutting it.".

AI has not yet upended hiring or billing in aggregate.

Recent findings suggest that the data suggest AI is not yet driving widespread staffing reductions. According to IDC, 57.9% of respondents stated AI has had no impact on their hiring, and more reported increasing hiring (24.2%) than decreasing it (9.2%).

"Many have predicted that AI will end the billable hour on the theory that faster work will lead clients to demand task-based billing," noted Horrigan. "The research indicates that has not happened broadly, at least not yet.".

The billable hour remains the most common primary billing method among law firms (45.7%), ahead of hybrid billing (31.8%), task-based billing (17.2%), and contingency fees (5.3%).

The research also points to cost savings, with 82.8% of respondents saying AI has saved their organization money.

AI becomes the baseline, not the differentiator.

The research indicates 80.5% of legal professionals and more than 91.0% of chief legal officers at the moment use AI in their legal work, and more than 99.0% of respondents either use it now or plan to within 12 months. The level of usage is also growing, with 93.0% of respondents saying they have increased their AI use, by an average of 65.0%, while just 0.9% have decreased it.

"When adoption ceilings sit above 90.0%, using AI stops being a differentiator and starts being a floor," remarked Ryan O'Leary, Research Director for Privacy and Legal Technology at IDC. "The advantage moves to how well it is used.".

Outlook on and adoption of AI differ by role.

According to data from The General Counsel Report, 86.8% of chief legal officers are very or somewhat optimistic about AI.

It has been revealed that judges, by contrast, are adopting AI at a slower pace. Data from the Relativity-NAWJ survey indicate 16.6% of respondents never use AI and another 33.3% use it only rarely. About one in five federal and state judges (20.4% and 20.0%, respectively) prohibit court staff from using AI, while 7.4% of federal judges and 14.2% of state judges permit and encourage it.

Their outlook is also more divided. In the Relativity-NAWJ survey, 47.1% of state court judges said they are very or somewhat optimistic, and 36.0% said they are very or somewhat concerned. Among federal judges surveyed by The Sedona Conference, 43.6% were optimistic, and 41.7% were concerned.

Accuracy beats speed, and trust beats cost.

In the IDC research, trust consistently outweighed speed and cost. When forced to choose, respondents favored accuracy over speed by 92.3% to 7.7%, and higher trust over lower cost by 79.3% to 20.7%. Respondents also preferred keeping a human in the loop (64.1%) over complete automation (35.9%).

It has been revealed that as AI agents enter legal workflows, the study indicates that oversight will determine whether trust keeps pace with adoption. For agentic AI, respondents stated human approval (67.0%) and mandatory source citations (60.0%) are the most commonly required safeguards.

Security posture (59.9%), governance capabilities (59.4%) and clear AI principles (51.9%) are the top three qualities legal professionals look for in AI vendors.

"Buyers aren't shopping for features first," mentioned O'Leary. "They're checking whether you're safe to let near their data.".

Inside organizations, governance work is still underway: about 91.0% have an AI governance framework in place or in progress, yet only 23.0% have fully adopted one, and 9.0% have no prepares at all, according to IDC's research.

According to recent reports, concerns about accuracy and data security remain the gatekeepers to deeper adoption. Hallucinations, which were not a leading concern in the 2024 study, are now respondents' top worry (52.0%), followed by data loss (46.0%) and data bias (41.0%). Yet hallucinations are also the risk legal professionals feel best equipped to handle: 44.7% say they are almost or fully prepared for them, and only 15.5% say they are not prepared at all.

To learn more about the findings in AI in Legal: 2026 Research Data, with research and analysis by IDC, download the full study here.

Its AI platform, Relativity aiR, transforms complex data into actionable insights at massive scale for litigation, investigations, regulatory inquiries, data breach responses, and other legal use cases. The world's largest law firms and corporations, government agencies, and a robust network of channel partners rely on Relativity's legal AI to securely surface and manage the most relevant and impactful information in their matters. The company also expands access to technology by providing its platform at no cost to academic institutions through its Relativity Academic program and to organizations supporting pro bono legal work through its Justice for Change initiative.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

Industry observers note that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Sources indicate that proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration blueprint and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It highlights how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:.

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole blueprint. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Recent findings suggest that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

It has been revealed that the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC highlighted almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Industry observers note that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

It has been revealed that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Industry observers note that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence reveals what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

It has been revealed that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives Young Kim (R-California) and Nikema Williams (D-Georgia) introduced this week the bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act, a bill that would streamline how certain foreclosed Federal Housing Administration (FHA) properties return to the market and direct a federal study of zero-down-payment FHA loans.

Under current law, differing federal requirements around partial claim liens can force servicers to pursue judicial foreclosures on some FHA loans even in nonjudicial foreclosure states, lengthening timelines and increasing legal costs before a vacant home can be resold.The bill, H.R. 11082, seeks to clarify how partial claim liens are treated following nonjudicial foreclosures for FHA-insured mortgages, bringing FHA authorities closer to those Congress granted the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (V.A.) home loan program last year.

“I’ve been proud to champion bipartisan legislation to alleviate the housing crisis and put the American Dream back within reach,” Rep. Kim mentioned in a statement. “My Housing Process Parity Act will build on these efforts by getting homes back on the market faster and exploring new pathways to homeownership for everyday Americans.”Williams said the limited stock of affordable homes is undermining families’ ability to build wealth. “The bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act cuts unnecessary barriers to get homes back on the market faster and expand housing supply,” she said. “Every family, no matter their ZIP code or bank account, deserves a fair shot at building wealth for the next generation.”.

The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) endorsed the bill, saying it “advances FHA program improvements, provides parity across government-insured mortgage programs, and supports broader efforts to expand access to sustainable homeownership,” according to a statement from MBA President and CEO Bob Broeksmit, CMB.

In a recent development, “Clarifying partial claim lien treatment following non-judicial foreclosures would provide greater certainty for servicers and lower costs for borrowers,” Broeksmit stated. “While foreclosure is never the desired outcome, a non-judicial process reduces legal costs, shortens timelines, and limits the financial impact on homeowners.”.

Beyond foreclosure process changes, the bill would require the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to study the feasibility of a newly introduced FHA-insured mortgage product with no down payment.

The study would examine potential benefits to low- and moderate-income and first-time buyers, as well as risks to taxpayers and the FHA Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, and identify safeguards needed to keep such loans sustainable.

Sources indicate that an Urban Institute analysis – authored by Alexei Alexandrov, Laurie Goodman, Ted Tozer and Sam Valverde – from earlier this year highlighted that moving from a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio range of 96% to 99% to a range of 100% to 104% LTVs raises the default probability by just 12 basis points — a difference the authors describe as statistically insignificant.“Allowing zero-down payment mortgages would level the playing field for potential homeowners without family wealth,” the researchers wrote in the report. “Moreover, FHA zero-down payment loans would also replace the inconsistent patchwork of down payment assistance programs.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

It has been revealed that his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health tech giant Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health intends that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

It has been revealed that kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”.

Recent findings suggest that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Recent findings suggest that searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

In a recent development, why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

Recent findings suggest that “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it indicates.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

It has been revealed that kelman, by his own account, is upcoming to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend stated I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman noted the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software organization he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”.

The Sojourn site indicates the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

It has been revealed that that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native manufacturer in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

According to recent reports, A new health blueprint typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a newly introduced mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He remarked at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

Recent findings suggest that he appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

Enterprise AI hits a wall of power and cooling, not GPU supply

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part.
  • It has been revealed that those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing.
  • “When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 07:55 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

It has been revealed that those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan noted. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”.

Hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

The economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan noted. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”.

In a recent development, SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the company builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent New Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

“You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”.

Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the firm’s AI and Cyber Lab.

Sources indicate that “It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

4 factors behind California's quakes, from the San Andreas to the Ring of Fire

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four factors explain California's constant shaking and why clusters of quakes can feel like a spike, from fault lines to depth.
  • Sources indicate that many Californians have felt the ground move more often lately, and a string of tremors has left them wondering whether something has changed beneath the state.
  • Even the quakes strong enough to make the news are a regular part of life in Southern California.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four factors explain California's constant shaking and why clusters of quakes can feel like a spike, from fault lines to depth.

Sources indicate that many Californians have felt the ground move more often lately, and a string of tremors has left them wondering whether something has changed beneath the state. Shaking is the ordinary condition of the region, and residents never notice nearly all of it. Southern California alone records about 10,000 earthquakes in a typical year, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), and only several hundred of them are stronger than magnitude 3.0. Most of the movement there is too faint for anyone to feel. A single quake that people do feel therefore stands out against a background that only seems quiet. The useful question is not whether California is shaking, because it always is. The question is what makes a particular run of quakes noticeable enough to feel like a surge.

Even the quakes strong enough to make the news are a regular part of life in Southern California. USGS estimates that the region has about 15 to 20 quakes above magnitude 4.0 in a typical year. A burst of such quakes also cannot tell anyone when a large one will strike. Pinning down the timing of a quake is “one of the most difficult unsolved problems in science,” Lillian Burkhard, lead author and a research affiliate at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, said, as reported by TIME.

USA TODAY set out to explain what was behind California’s recent jump in earthquake activity. Its reasons include the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific’s Ring of Fire, and the depth at which a quake begins. Some are permanent features of the land that explain why California always shakes. Others explain how one quake becomes a cluster, or why a whole city feels it. None of them indicates that the ground under California has become more active.

Central California's recent cluster of tremors happened along the state's best-known fault line. Those tremors struck a stretch of ground directly next to the San Andreas Fault, close to Highway 25, according to USA TODAY. Much of California lies along that fault, which, TIME reports, extends from the Salton Sea to San Francisco. With a fault that long under so much of the state, quakes beside it are an ordinary part of life there and not a sign of change. The fault explains why the ground moved in that spot, but it does not show that a large rupture is coming.

It has been revealed that the part of the fault that concerns seismologists is the southern section, where the San Andreas meets the San Jacinto Fault and where strain has been accumulating for generations. TIME reports that the two faults are under more stress than at any time since the 11th century, and that the last major quake to ease stress in the system they share came 160 years ago. The 20 million people who live along the two faults face that stored strain, and it deserves far more of their attention than any single cluster of tremors.

Much of what feels like a run of separate quakes is often one rupture and the smaller quakes around it. Near Pinnacles in central California, two smaller quakes came before a magnitude 5.0 mainshock, and more tremors came after it, according to USA TODAY. A news feed may list each of those tremors as its own event, but all of them trace back to a single break in the ground. Counted one at a time, they suggest a fault that is getting busier.

Recent findings suggest that the label “foreshock” is given only after a larger quake arrives. The two early quakes near Pinnacles looked like any other minor quake at the time. The familiar shape of a sequence, with small quakes building to a large one and then tapering off, can be seen only after it has ended. That shape is a description of the past, not a forecast.

California shakes first because of where it sits on the planet. Of all the earthquakes on Earth, 90% occur along the Ring of Fire, a band that stretches 25,000 miles around the edge of the Pacific Ocean and takes in California, according to USA TODAY. Only 5% to 6% of the world’s quakes happen along the Alpide belt, the next most active zone, according to USGS. California’s quakes belong to a pattern far larger than the state itself.

Sources indicate that the belt is the reason California always shakes, and for that reason it cannot explain a sudden rise. Instruments around the world pick up an estimated 500,000 earthquakes in a year, according to USGS, and most happen on the belt that runs through California. The San Andreas Fault is this same belt seen up close in one state, so the two are one explanation at two scales, not separate causes.

The worst case is a rupture on the San Andreas that continues into the San Jacinto Fault, and that could happen at only one spot. Cajon Pass is the only point where the two faults intersect, TIME reports, and the faults cross there far below the surface. “A rupture crossing from one region to the other requires favorable conditions at depth,” Burkhard stated. Tremors felt elsewhere along the fault cannot show whether a rupture will get through that crossing point, or when.

The San Andreas is a long-term danger to prepare for, not a reason to panic over every new tremor.

It has been revealed that the size of the cluster depends on who counted the tremors and over what stretch of time. One tally, from Fox Weather, puts the tremors after the mainshock at more than a dozen. KSBW reports only six aftershocks, along with a mainshock that the U.S. Geological Survey first measured at magnitude 5.1 and later revised down to 5.0. Early numbers in any sequence are provisional and settle only as reports come in. A spike built from these counts is partly a matter of bookkeeping, and the same rupture can be logged as a handful of quakes or as more than a dozen.

Before reading a burst of quakes as a trend, a reader should ask how many separate ruptures it contains, and often the answer is one.

The recent quake in Los Angeles began only about 10 miles below the surface, and that shallow start is why people throughout the city felt it, according to USA TODAY. A shallow source of this kind is part of the area's usual pattern. In 2024, a different quake near Malibu, Calif., started at a similar depth of about 8 miles underground, according to U.S. Geological Survey figures reported by The Associated Press. Depth explains why so many people noticed the quake, not whether the ground has grown more active. When a shallow source puts a routine quake in front of an entire city, a few in a row are enough to make ordinary activity feel like a spike.

A quake that people across a whole region feel can still be ordinary to the scientists who study the ground. "It's sort of run of the mill for earthquake country," seismologist Lucy Jones noted of the 2024 Malibu quake, as reported by The Associated Press. The number of people who notice a quake tells no one whether it will do harm. Real harm in Los Angeles has come from much larger quakes, and 64 people died in the magnitude 6.6 San Fernando earthquake in 1971. The danger of a quake depends on its size, not on how far across a city people feel it.

A shallow quake that everyone feels is a sign of where it began, not a sign that a bigger one is coming.

The Ring of Fire will remain long after any burst of quakes fades, which makes it a fact about where Californians live, not about what is changing.

Industry observers note that crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Sources indicate that total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

In a recent development, the current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

According to recent reports, that monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

It has been revealed that bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

It has been revealed that this time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

According to recent reports, A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot demonstrates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot demonstrates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

It has been revealed that blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham states those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

It has been revealed that if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

Sources indicate that it shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own people. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

Industry observers note that while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what owners hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

Recent findings suggest that the striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Recent findings suggest that compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It demonstrates the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

In a recent development, binance indicates the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

In a recent development, what it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

In a recent development, what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

Shiba Inu’s 1.7 million holder milestone arrived when SHIB was trading at about $0.00000382, following a 0.78% decline over the last day.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

According to recent reports, upgrade, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA remarked Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

According to recent reports, in its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

In a recent development, that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA stated it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA remarked. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

In a recent development, ULA stated Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based manufacturer hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

It has been revealed that “It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and Fresh Glenn for our return to flight.”.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Upcoming Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller noted before the flight.

It has been revealed that before Sunday, Amazon had debuted 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

It has been revealed that amazon has stated it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#18684. America builds cool things, except houses

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (972 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

America builds cool things, except houses

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If housing were an importable product, most American homebuilders would be out of business.
  • We no longer know how to build a quality product at an affordable price, and we’re approaching a crisis that may finally force change.
  • When the American auto industry fell behind, higher-quality imports pressured Detroit to innovate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If housing were an importable product, most American homebuilders would be out of business. Because it isn’t, our industry has never faced the competitive pressure that drives innovation. Decades of rising home prices have made matters worse. When buyers tolerate every cost increase, nothing pushes us to cut costs.

We no longer know how to build a quality product at an affordable price, and we’re approaching a crisis that may finally force change.

When the American auto industry fell behind, higher-quality imports pressured Detroit to innovate. Detroit may have lost market share, but Americans could still get quality cars. If the American homebuilding industry can no longer supply affordable housing, it raises questions about whether homes fit the model of the type of product the USA excels at building.

It has been revealed that america’s reign of manufacturing dominance took place during an era when most of the everyday objects we’d now call “products” weren’t manufactured in the modern sense – they were made at home or by local artisans. We excelled at mass-producing novel and exciting products like cars or firearms. By contrast, China’s contemporary manufacturing dominance built a world where almost every household object that exists is industrially manufactured.

Sources indicate that american manufacturing is still the second largest globally, but our dominance applies to sophisticated products like monoclonal antibodies, jet engines, and advanced industrial machines. If a proposed product has near-magical requirements and a large enough R&D budget, we’re the right country to produce it, but we’ve never held anything like China’s role as the dominant mass producer of cheap, quotidian consumer goods.

Recent findings suggest that the products the US manufactures competitively are typically regulated very differently from upcoming homes. The FAA doesn’t require Boeing to use quarter-inch titanium rivets spaced one and a half inches apart. Instead, it lets manufacturers compete to engineer solutions that meet performance standards set cooperatively by a group of industry stakeholders. Many nations use performance-based standards in their housing codes, and stricter standards don’t have to mean less affordable housing. Japan is often cited as a success story for maintaining housing affordability despite having some of the world’s most demanding seismic standards.

Another major regulatory barrier limits where housing gets built. After World War II, federally subsidized highways and mortgages made the car-oriented suburb the default, and cities rewrote their zoning codes to reflect that model. Minimum lot sizes, deep setbacks, density caps, and parking requirements effectively banned the “missing middle” housing that once met demand in the most desirable areas. Instead of letting neighborhoods grow through small, continuous infill, zoning froze them in place and pushed upcoming growth outward.

Under these rules, housing development is now effectively squeezed into just two viable business models: the large-scale suburban single-family homebuilder, and the institutional apartment developer. Both models require large swathes of vacant land where they can run the repeatable processes of a century-old mass manufacturing model.

Recent findings suggest that manufacturing has moved on. The art of producing boring things at hyperscale is a uniquely Chinese invention built around a state-orchestrated model of supply chain networks featuring industrial clustering and dynamic capacity pooling. Widespread adoption of the right technology could coordinate labor resources and supply chains to maximize network resource efficiency. Before any of that matters, we have to admit that the housing we’ve been building isn’t good enough.

Sources indicate that nobody will drive by a contemporary master planned community in a hundred years to admire its architecture. Almost every American production homebuilder returning from a European vacation has had the same unsettling feeling that not a single home we spent our careers building will still be standing a hundred years after we die. Builders have so little unique brand identity that a customer driving through a new development has to rely entirely on marketing signage to know when they’ve left one builder’s tract and entered another’s.

Customers are opting out of choosing between buying in a dull, exurban neighborhood and renting an overpriced “luxury” 5-over-1 apartment building in a more desirable area. They want it cheap and they want it good. When the available housing presents insufficient value, they double up with roommates or family.

Recent findings suggest that unique designs carry a level of risk that’s largely incompatible with the scale of the predominant business models. Even in Hollywood, a few low-budget originals have begun outperforming franchise blockbusters. If buyers are opting out of what we’ve been building, maybe it’s time we built something more congruent with what we’re good at building: products with nearly magical requirements. A home that’s affordable, durable, and worth admiring a hundred years from now is exactly that kind of product.

Industry observers note that people with the means and knowledge to build their own quirky homes have captivated social media onlookers with Earthships, Quonset huts, geodesic domes, and structures made from compressed earth bricks, straw bales, and all manner of materials that are wildly unsuited to production homebuilding. None of those methods is likely to scale, but each of those wacky homes is a testament to the creativity we’re capable of. Our business models leave that creativity nowhere to go.

In a recent development, what might housing look like if we took more risks? Emerging technologies are enabling the rapid iteration of newly introduced designs and accelerating the administrative processes behind bidding out new product. Builders could take more chances on small projects built differently. A small bet that fails costs little, and one that succeeds can prove out a profitable model worth repeating.

Recent findings suggest that as a nation, we’ve never done our best work on bland things. We’re at our best when we’re solving a nearly impossible problem or designing something enduringly lovable. It’s time we treated the attainable American home as one of those problems.

Africa Tech Festival, the continent's longest-running and most influential technology gathering, concluded its 29th edition at the Cape Town International Convention Centre, welcoming more than 15,000 delegates over the three days.

According to recent reports, CAPE TOWN, South Africa, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI is opening up opportunities for African businesses to improve performance, develop new revenue streams and equip young people for a changing workplace. This was a central theme as Africa Tech Festival (www.AfricaTechFestival.com) 2026 concluded in Cape Town yesterday, with industry leaders sharing how digitalisation is changing the way companies operate, create jobs and broaden access to digital services.

Providing an enterprise perspective, Frederik Zietsman, Group CEO of Takealot, opened the final day's headline programme in conversation with Tomiwa Aladekomo, CEO of Substantial Cabal Media. Their discussion explored the realities of building a profitable e-commerce business in South Africa, including the importance of customer trust and investment in the infrastructure needed to reach consumers. "It starts and ends with trust. Because if you don't have trust, then ultimately, you fail," said Zietsman. He described how Takealot has invested in its own delivery infrastructure and developed a network of approximately 20,000 personal shoppers to help consumers in underserved communities access online retail.

Recent findings suggest that turning to Africa's role in the AI economy, Hardy Pemhiwa, President and Group CEO of Cassava Technologies, discussed how to make innovation more accessible and help local ideas reach wider markets. "I really would love to see an Africa where innovation is not limited by traditional education," he said, noting that AI could help overcome language barriers that have historically prevented promising ideas from being commercialised. Martin Manniche, CEO of AXON Networks, considered the role of automation and cloud-native technologies in modernising telecommunications infrastructure to support sophisticated digital services.

Industry observers note that as technology changes how businesses operate, it is also changing the skills employers need and the opportunities available to young people. Charles Murito, Regional Director, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Sub-Saharan Africa at Google; Tiara Pathon, AI Skills Director at Microsoft; and Ziyad Cassim, Group CEO of UVU Africa, examined the implications for Africa's workforce. Murito asked how young people can move from being job seekers to value creators, advocating entrepreneurship and latest sources of employment. Pathon challenged conventional approaches to training, saying that "organisations like ours need to stop treating learners as beneficiaries of learning, and see them as participants and creators." Cassim warned that "the biggest risk we're seeing right now is young people losing that first opportunity to work," calling on employers to give young talent opportunities to gain practical experience.

However, the growing use of AI also raises questions about accountability when technology fails. Lawrence Matemba, Chief Policy Analyst and Deputy Director-General in the South African Presidency, and Geoff Okao, Chief Digital Officer and Deputy Director, Digital Impact at UNICEF, examined who should be held accountable when automated decisions cause harm. Matemba argued that organisations providing services must accept responsibility for failures, emphasising that citizens must remain central to the design and delivery of those services. Okao cautioned that "a risk register does not by default protect the person who's harmed", calling for safeguards that consider the people affected, not just the risks facing organisations.

It has been revealed that access to finance was another area of discussion, with SME funding among dozens of topics explored across the festival's nine content stages. On the fintech stage, executives from Makko Brothers Credit Limited, Nomba, Edge Growth and Absa Corporate and Investment Bank examined alternative lending models, transaction-based credit assessments and ways to improve access to working capital.

Africa Tech Festival, the continent's longest-running and most influential technology gathering, concluded its 29th edition at the Cape Town International Convention Centre, welcoming more than 15,000 delegates over the three days.

"This week we've heard from government leaders, technology companies, investors and entrepreneurs on complications ranging from digital sovereignty and infrastructure investment to AI governance, business growth and skills development. Africa Tech Festival provides a platform for these different perspectives to come together, forging connections and partnerships that will help drive the industry forward," remarked David Monaghan, Vice President, Africa Tech Festival.

Through six core pillars spanning connectivity, AI, cybersecurity, data centres, digital transformation and the startup ecosystem, Africa Tech Festival delivers a comprehensive view of the trends, challenges and opportunities defining Africa's digital landscape.

Does your brokerage need a mortgage servicing arm to keep past clients engaged?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2026, mortgage servicing became one of the real estate brokerage industry’s must have ancillary services.
  • For Peter Voss, the broker-owner of 3% Listing Co.,  Rocket Companies’ acquisitions of Redfin and Mr.Cooper in mid-2025 was a real wake up call as to what true vertical integration looks like.
  • Industry observers note that “That was like the blinders coming off for everyone,” Voss stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2026, mortgage servicing became one of the real estate brokerage industry’s must have ancillary services.

For Peter Voss, the broker-owner of 3% Listing Co.,  Rocket Companies’ acquisitions of Redfin and Mr.Cooper in mid-2025 was a real wake up call as to what true vertical integration looks like.

Industry observers note that “That was like the blinders coming off for everyone,” Voss stated. “It was like ‘Holy cow! That is real vertical integration.’ It was just so different from what everyone else had been thinking about.”.

This move by Rocket was followed in 2026 by eXp Realty’s mortgage joint venture with Newrez, Revenos Mortgage, which includes a servicing component, and HomeServices of America adding in-house mortgage servicing through its wholly owned lender, Prosperity Home Mortgage, LLC.

At the time of the launch, Chris Kelly, the CEO of the RealTrends Verified HomeServices of America, told HousingWire that the company decided to venture into servicing because they were “increasingly seeing that loans end up with a servicer and those servicers are moving further upstream.”.

“It used to be that a broker started a mortgage company, but now mortgage companies are starting real estate companies and the whole point of it is to use that servicing to try and siphon off that business and acquire home buyer and seller clients before they even start browsing for homes on a search portal,” Kelly told HousingWire in late summer.

It has been revealed that but for smaller, regional brokerages owning a mortgage servicer is not an option. However, this doesn’t mean that they have given up in their efforts to stay top of mind with past clients.

According to recent reports, instead of venturing into mortgage servicing, Voss said 3% Listing Co. has employed a variety of strategies to ensure his organization is the one past clients turn to when it is time to move, from a home value tool that allows homeowners to see the estimated value of their property without having to talk to an agent to reminders about seasonal home maintenance.

In a recent development, “We just sent out an email ahead of the winter season reminding people to unhook their outdoor hoses,” Voss remarked. “It’s really small things like that, trying to be real and making sure what we are doing is beneficial to past clients.”.

Voss mentioned his firm is also exploring a partnership with an HVAC filter organization that sends homeowners latest filters every three months when it’s time to swap out filters.

“We’re looking at the possibility of setting it up as a closing gift for clients where every three months they get a filter in the mail that is branded to us,” he said. “We want to think outside of the box because just because everyone else is doing things one way doesn’t mean we have to.”.

Home Handoff is a proptech organization focused on helping agents and their clients manage their home transition, provides home sellers with a structured space to provide information regarding property utilities, renovations and service providers that can then be shared with buyers or prospective buyers. The firm is all about finding different ways for agents to keep their name in front of past clients. The company is working with agents, teams and brokerages, to put their own branding on the “home handbook” the company provides clients with. In addition to information regarding the property, agents can also provide links to vetted service professionals such as contractors, landscapers and pet sitters.

Recent findings suggest that “The whole platform is built to keep the agent as the hero. Every time the seller or buyer logs into the platform they see it is provided by their agent or their brokerage,” Cody Bartkoski, the CEO of Home Handoff, said.

In New York City, Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, is also employing different means of maintaining relationships with clients. The firm, which does not own any ancillary services operations, instead operates an advertising arm that works with trusted mortgage and title professionals to create content from podcasts, to blog posts to short video series.

According to Matt Leone, BHS’s chief marketing officer, the primary goal of this marketing and advertising program is to educate viewers and listeners and that they are not creating content just for the sake of “generating clicks.” He added that they don’t necessarily view these efforts as a lead generation tool, but as a way to get their “name out there as a thought leader.”.

“You don’t want it to be a traditional ad message,” Leone said. “You want it to be through your thought leadership, your insights and being seen as an expert that you earn these opportunities.”.

Leone added that consumers encounter so many different advertisements each day that many just tune out that type of content.

According to recent reports, “We want to educate them, both consumers and agents, with the individuals in those spaces that are the most knowledgeable,” Leone mentioned. “We work with our agents to find the providers that are the best at their craft and we see if they’d be interested in collaborating with us.”.

While regional firms like 3% Listing Co. and BHS may not have mortgage servicers or even a stable of ancillary services within their firm, they are still finding meaningful ways to engage with and keep their names in front of consumers.

In a recent development, “It isn’t just about handing out branded T-shirts to people, but about how you connect with them and give the T-shirt value so that people are going to reuse it,” Voss stated. “I think that is where a lot of brokerages are struggling. They’re trying to find that additional income stream and where that additional lead source is, but without a whole lot of added cost.”.

Inaccurate, incomplete, and inconsistent data can undermine business decisions and create costly inefficiencies. Data quality solutions help organizations maintain accurate, complete, and consistent data across applications, databases, and cloud environments. Capabilities such as data profiling, cleansing, validation, standardization, duplicate detection, and ongoing quality monitoring also help IT and data teams identify and resolve errors, establish quality standards, and support governance requirements. The greatest value comes from ensuring that the data supporting operations, analytics, automation, and AI is reliable enough to deliver the intended business outcomes.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella noted the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

According to recent reports, “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

In a recent development, it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

In a recent development, no doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks, but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with intends to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

Meantime, Huang noted he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more organization now. Maybe those guys (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

In a recent development, palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute this week $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks.

Next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Georgia-based homebuilder My Home Communities is expanding beyond its home state with fresh-home communities planned in South Carolina, Alabama and Northwest Florida, the tech giant unveiled earlier this week.

The privately held builder, founded in 2018, will launch sales this month at Stonebrook in Gaffney, South Carolina, is planning an 89-homesite community in Summerdale, Alabama, and is preparing an initial presence along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton, Florida.

Sources indicate that “Georgia has provided an incredible foundation for our firm, and we’re excited to take what we’ve built here into fresh markets,” mentioned Jacob Prather, president of My Home Communities. “Expanding into South Carolina, Alabama and Florida is about building relationships, creating new opportunities for homebuyers and establishing My Home Communities as a recognized homebuilding brand throughout the Southeast.”.

My Home Communities focused its first eight years on establishing a footprint across metro Atlanta and other Georgia markets, offering single-family homes and communities targeted to a wide range of buyers.

The tech giant remarked continued investment in Georgia remains a core part of its strategy even as it exports its building processes and customer service model to other Southeast states.

According to recent reports, the expansion is being supported by the Tamra Wade Team, backed by RE/MAX TRU, which is leading sales and marketing efforts for My Home Communities in the new markets. The team has worked with the builder for several years in Georgia, providing continuity as the firm introduces its brand to buyers outside the state.

In South Carolina, Stonebrook in Gaffney is preparing to launch sales in November 2026, with prices expected to start in the high $200,000s, according to the organization. The community is My Home Communities’ first project in South Carolina.

In Alabama, The Retreat in Summerdale is planned as an 89-homesite community. Sales timing has not yet been revealed. The manufacturer remarked the project will expand its reach into the Gulf Coast corridor, where latest-home demand has been supported by employment growth and relative affordability compared to coastal metros.

In Northwest Florida, My Home Communities looks to start with two homesites along Hamilton Bridge Road in Milton. Additional community details and sales timelines will be released later.

In a recent development, “Our growth is intentional, and we’re focused on finding the right opportunities in markets where we believe our homes and communities will resonate with buyers,” Prather said. “With Stonebrook launching sales this month and additional communities planned in Alabama and Florida, we’re excited to introduce our brand to newly introduced audiences.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Legacy Motor Club, the NASCAR team that Jimmie Johnson, a seven-time Cup Series champion, owns, wrapped up an $85 million fundraising round headed by Knighthead Capital Management, according to Bloomberg.

The round puts Legacy's worth at $450 million, according to Bloomberg, which attributed the figure to a source with knowledge of the deal who lacked permission to discuss it in public.

According to recent reports, legacy will put the money toward growing its operation and building a upcoming headquarters in Mooresville, North Carolina, according to Bloomberg. The headquarters is expected to open in 2028.

Sources indicate that in July, Legacy revealed an earlier capital raise backed by investors such as Philadelphia Phillies player Bryce Harper, tennis champion Andy Roddick, musician Darius Rucker and chef Guy Fieri, according to Bloomberg. Johnson told Bloomberg that Legacy returned to investors for additional capital so it could keep expanding.

Johnson said the investment positions Legacy to reach its goal of being "a tier one racing operation in the Nascar series," according to Bloomberg.

Legacy operates three NASCAR teams with charters, and each of them runs the Toyota $TM Camry XSE. Josh Berry, Erik Jones and Riley Herbst will drive for the team in the coming season, according to Bloomberg.

Knighthead's leader is co-founder Tom Wagner, who introduced the investment organization back in 2008. Wagner is also a part owner of both the Las Vegas Raiders and Birmingham City Football Club, according to Bloomberg.

Bloomberg noted that Knighthead bought into Legacy in January 2025, taking a minority stake by purchasing a large portion of the shares airline entrepreneur Maury Gallagher held. That transaction made Johnson the team's majority owner.

Kyle Kneisly, a Knighthead partner and Legacy board member, told Bloomberg that deploying growth capital was part of the plan from the start.

Sources indicate that the fresh round follows NASCAR's settlement of a federal antitrust lawsuit with Michael Jordan's 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports. The settlement made charters permanent for NASCAR teams, a change that could raise the worth of clubs, according to Bloomberg.
