One year after debuting as a Challenger and Outperformer, Sprocket earns perfect scores on four criteria as it pairs expert pentesters with a fleet of AI agents.

MADISON, Wis., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sprocket Security has been named a Leader in the GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS) v5. Sprocket placed as a Leader in the report's Agile Optimizers scorecards and earned perfect marks on test launch efficiency, attack surface integration, rules of engagement controls, and the testing audit trail.

The placement marks a clear step up from 2025, when GigaOm recognized Sprocket as a Challenger and Outperformer. In the year between, Sprocket expanded its capabilities with a fleet of AI agents that work alongside its pentesters, extending how much of the attack surface gets tested and how quickly.

This year's report, authored by GigaOm analyst Chris Ray, maps four buyer profiles to four quadrants. It frames five market themes around the questions buyers should ask before signing: who performs the test, how it reaches internal networks, and what evidence an auditor will accept?

"Sprocket Security earns its Leader position by pairing AI testing agents with human validation of every finding, and wrapping both in machine-enforced scope, a customer kill switch and a checksummed audit trail, so its testing keeps pace with a changing attack surface without giving up control," Ray shared.

Sprocket's top scores reflect how the platform runs day to day:.

Test launch efficiency (5.0): Teams scope and start testing without weeks of kickoff calls and paperwork.

Attack surface integration (5.0): Testing follows the attack surface as it changes, so fresh assets get tested as they appear.

Rules of engagement controls (5.0): Customers set what gets tested, when, and how, with guardrails built into the platform.

Testing audit trail (5.0): Every action is logged, giving security teams and auditors a record of what was tested and what was found.

Expert Pentesters, Now With an AI Fleet.

Sprocket was founded because point-in-time pentests couldn't keep up with how companies change. Continuous testing closed part of that gap. Sprocket's AI agents close more of it, running alongside its pentesters on the Sprocket platform:.

Apex: an agentic pentester for unauthenticated web applications, mapping each app and testing its own theories about where it might break.

Link: an agentic pentester for authenticated web applications, testing what sits behind the login.

Pinion: an agentic pentester for internal networks, falling the attack paths worth chasing.

Sprocket's pentesters direct the work and validate what the agents find, so customers get more coverage without trading away the judgment of an experienced tester.

"A year ago GigaOm called us a Challenger. Today we are a Leader, and agentic innovation is why. We put a fleet of AI agents to work next to our pentesters for all types of testing, and the results show up in these scores," stated Casey Cammilleri, CEO and founder of Sprocket Security. "Buyers are asking who is actually testing, whether it reaches the parts of the network attackers go after, and whether the results will hold up with an auditor. Our answer is experienced pentesters with agents that extend their reach, on a platform that highlights its work.".

Organizations that work with Sprocket Security get:.

Sprocket will keep expanding its AI fleet and testing coverage. Every new agent is held to Sprocket's Safety Framework for Autonomous Offensive Security Agents, which requires agents to stay within scope, stop at proof, log every action, and let humans step in at any point. The aim is to give buyers clear answers to the questions GigaOm says to ask: who is testing, how far the testing reaches, and what evidence it leaves behind.

Security leaders can access a complimentary copy of the GigaOm Radar for Penetration Testing as a Service v5 at https://www.sprocketsecurity.com/gigaom.

According to recent reports, sprocket Security provides a technology-powered continuous penetration testing platform. Named in GigaOm and Gartner reports this year, Sprocket continuously monitors customer environments and triggers hybrid testing based on each customer's dynamic attack surface and emerging threats. Unlike legacy penetration testing, Sprocket's continuous approach delivers real-time insights and adaptive security, giving organizations a security posture that reflects today, not their last test.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon.
  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club revealed Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a fresh job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club revealed Tuesday.

Industry observers note that “His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation organization toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew noted his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

According to recent reports, “In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Recent findings suggest that chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he noted. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he mentioned.

Industry observers note that talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew notes he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

Recent findings suggest that he recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew noted he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

It has been revealed that the bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew remarked. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

In a recent development, “It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

In a recent development, the Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pulley, a development technology tech giant that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in upcoming funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company unveiled this week.

Sources indicate that the financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. Pulley said the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and latest products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines.

Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.

In a recent development, pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The firm estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions.

In a recent development, “The speed at which we build is one of the most important challenges facing America over the next decade,” remarked Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”.

Pulley stated it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The manufacturer reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time.

Pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction plan reviews and coordination with local agencies. The organization also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building prepares directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement.

In a recent development, the company said customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission.

According to recent reports, with the new funding, Pulley intends to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs.

Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance problems earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during plan check.

Lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing quickly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital plans and delay unit delivery into tight markets.

Tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and new capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private blueprint review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech.
  • The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD noted in a blog post last week.

It’s a massive upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD stated a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Industry observers note that nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the firm’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. Fresh York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Industry observers note that back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves.
  • In a recent development, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

In a recent development, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The firm says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

Industry observers note that the project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery stated the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it massive" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

In a recent development, the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

According to recent reports, the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he remarked, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

In a recent development, the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

Sources indicate that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Industry observers note that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent manufacturer, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

Sources indicate that this background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU rolled out earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on organization disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

It has been revealed that for everyday owners, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

According to recent reports, the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

Recent findings suggest that eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

According to recent reports, shares of Morgan Stanley $MS and Goldman Sachs $GS each fell more than 10% this week, placing them among the index's worst performers, according to Bloomberg. Both banks hold top roles on Anthropic's IPO.

Bank stocks fell on Friday, when heavy selling of artificial-intelligence shares unsettled markets worldwide.

In a recent development, financial stocks slid on Thursday after JPMorgan $JPM Chase, Visa $V and Mastercard $MA disclosed that an attack targeting one of their vendors had exposed certain customers' details, according to Bloomberg. That followed earlier disruptions this week, including an outage at the National Security Agency's internal communications network and a "technical matter" at JPMorgan, according to Bloomberg.

In a recent development, "Bank stocks are getting hit by a confluence of macro concerns rather than anything fundamentally newly introduced with the banks themselves," Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan mentioned, according to Bloomberg. "The broader risk-off move in technology hasn't helped either, particularly for capital-markets-oriented banks.".

Chan also pointed to inflation and the Federal Reserve. "Persistent inflation has put higher-for-longer rates back at the forefront, with Fed officials raising the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December," he remarked, according to Bloomberg. "Renewed geopolitical tensions around Iran are adding another layer of uncertainty and could complicate the inflation outlook through energy prices.".

Industry observers note that the KBW index formed a "death cross" on Thursday, a bearish technical signal that may point to more short-term weakness, according to Bloomberg. Bank stocks have given back all of the advance they had built up since January.

Recent findings suggest that the sector was already under pressure before this week. In October, the index was headed for a sixth straight weekly loss and had fallen 13% from its August record, putting it in correction territory. Worries about how artificial intelligence will disrupt financial services were weighing on the stocks then.

A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Latest York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research remarked that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that according to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Company, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

It has been revealed that according to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs said that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under New York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

According to recent reports, they "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the Latest York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins.".

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, mentioned that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them.".

According to recent reports, critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also remarked that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the manufacturer’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” noted Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the manufacturer’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he noted.

Sources indicate that the full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” consumers of each manufacturer’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

It has been revealed that the numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

Fresh MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella declared that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

In a recent development, the lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft indicates it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it notes matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other newly introduced models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

Sources indicate that the other latest business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Firm consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

According to recent reports, keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he stated.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A latest Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

According to recent reports, in another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.
